newsitem.title: GERMANY: Expellees reject draft German-Czech declaration.
newsitem.headline: Expellees reject draft German-Czech declaration.

text.p: Ethnic Germans expelled from Czech territory after World War Two on Tuesday vowed to resist a draft German-Czech declaration intended to end years of mutual resentment, saying it simply swept problems under the carpet.

In the draft text, expected to be initialled by foreign ministers next week, both countries admit to injustices done during the 1938-45 Nazi occupation of Czechoslovakia and its aftermath, but skirt issues of compensation for both Czech and ethnic German victims.

"A solution has not been brought closer for any of the questions which remain open in German-Czech relations," said Fritz Wittmann, president of the expellees' association BdV which has been one of the biggest obstacles to the declaration.
"The expellees will not let themselves be deterred from continuing their people's diplomacy to achieve justice and reconciliation," his statement added.

Wittmann was angry that the draft text offers no prospect of direct compensation for 2.5 million "Sudeten Germans" who were accused en masse of welcoming the Nazi occupation and were expelled, often brutally, after the war.
Instead, Prague admits innocent people suffered injustice in the expulsion, while Germany apologises for Nazi brutality.

There was no immediate comment from the expellees' political mentor, the Bavarian-based CSU which is part of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition and has in the past hinted Bonn should resist Czech EU membership until the expellees are satisfied.
Bonn also had no comment on the draft, which was leaked in Prague and which Germany had not planned to publish yet.
But German media welcomed the text, the product of almost two years of talks, as the best that could be achieved in difficult circumstances.

The declaration aims to set aside the only major issue still outstanding between Germany and the neighbours the Nazis occupied between 1938 and 1945, and pave the way for the Czech Republic to join the European Union and NATO in the years ahead.

"Prague is at least for the first time ready explicitly to regret the expulsion of Sudeten Germans and the unatoned-for excesses which also took place on the Czech side," national ARD television news said in an editorial.

"It's unfortunate that the victims on both sides have little to show for it. There will be no compensation for the victims of Nazi rule or for Sudeten Germans, let alone a right for those who were driven out to return to their homeland. With the best will in the world, more couldn't be expected," it added.

Germany is to contribute most of a 160 million mark fund for projects to help victims of the war, but there is no mention of personal compensation of the kind which has been paid to victims of the Nazis in Poland and other countries.
Both countries agree to respect each other's laws on the wartime issues, in effect ruling out claims by ethnic Germans against expropriations which Prague's "Benes decrees" declared legal.
Wittmann accused both sides of deliberately leaving aside the most sensitive issues.
"Instead they declare that they do not want to burden their relations with them...

"How can the German government take responsibility for the fact that it has decided...to override universal human rights and the illegality of expulsions, genocide, expropriation without compensation and the right to a homeland?" he asked.
"There is no statute of limitations on crimes against humanity. Claims on (lost) property and wealth do not expire along with the generation of those who experienced the events."
